Honeycomb
HUN-ee-kohm
noun
From honey and comb, the waxen cells wrought by bees; hence honey still in its comb, unstrained — the sweetest form of the sweetest thing the ancient table knew.

Biblical Definition

The honeycomb is honey still in the wax, taken from the rock or the wild wood and eaten unstrained — and Scripture always means by it something sweeter than sweet. The Psalmist ranks the judgments of the LORD above gold, “sweeter also than honey and the honeycomb” (Psa 19:10), so that the comb becomes the measure by which the word of God exceeds every earthly pleasure. Proverbs applies it to speech: “Pleasant words are as an honeycomb, sweet to the soul, and health to the bones” (Pro 16:24), and warns that the lips of a strange woman also drop as an honeycomb while her end is bitter as wormwood (Pro 5:3-4) — sweetness is no proof of safety. The full soul loatheth an honeycomb, but to the hungry soul every bitter thing is sweet (Pro 27:7), which is the whole doctrine of spiritual appetite in one line. In the Song, the Bridegroom says, “I have eaten my honeycomb with my honey” (Son 5:1), and the bride’s lips drop as the honeycomb (Son 4:11). But the greatest occurrence is the plainest. On the evening of the resurrection, when the disciples believed not for joy and wondered, the risen Christ asked, “Have ye here any meat?” and they gave Him a piece of a broiled fish, and of an honeycomb, “and he took it, and did eat before them” (Luk 24:42-43). A spirit hath not flesh and bones. The honeycomb is evidence.

Webster 1828 Definition

The waxen cells wrought by bees, filled with honey; in Scripture the measure of the word’s sweetness, and part of the risen Christ’s supper.

HONEYCOMB, the waxen structure of cells formed by bees for the reception of honey.

From honey and comb; honey in the comb, unstrained.

The judgments of the LORD are sweeter than honey and the honeycomb (Psa 19:10).

Pleasant words are as an honeycomb, sweet to the soul, and health to the bones (Pro 16:24).

The risen Lord ate of a broiled fish and of an honeycomb before His disciples (Luk 24:42-43).

Key Scripture

Psa 19:10 — "More to be desired are they than gold, yea, than much fine gold: sweeter also than honey and the honeycomb."

Pro 27:7 — "The full soul loatheth an honeycomb; but to the hungry soul every bitter thing is sweet."

Son 5:1 — "I am come into my garden, my sister, my spouse: I have gathered my myrrh with my spice; I have eaten my honeycomb with my honey; I have drunk my wine with my milk: eat, O friends; drink, yea, drink abundantly, O beloved."

Luk 24:43 — "And he took it, and did eat before them."

Modern Corruption

The honeycomb of Luke 24 is quietly set aside wherever the resurrection is reduced to a spiritual impression in the disciples’ hearts rather than a body raised.

expand to see more

The corruption is ancient and modern at once. The ancient form was docetism and the Gnostic denial that Christ had a true body at all; the modern form is the liberal-Protestant reduction of the resurrection to a symbol — Bultmann’s dictum that Jesus rose into the kerygma, Schleiermacher’s inward Christ, and the popular pulpit version in which Easter means that love survives death or that hope always returns in spring. Luke closes that door with a piece of fish and a piece of honeycomb. The Lord did not merely appear; He asked for food, took it, and ate it before them, having first said, Behold my hands and my feet, that it is I myself: handle me, and see; for a spirit hath not flesh and bones, as ye see me have (Luk 24:39). Eating is the one thing an apparition cannot do. The honeycomb is therefore not a domestic detail but an apologetic: the same body that was crucified, glorified and no longer subject to death, was in that room and consumed ordinary food. Deny it and the whole gospel falls, for if Christ be not raised, your faith is vain, ye are yet in your sins (1Co 15:17).

Recover both edges of the comb. Toward Christ: the risen body is the pledge of ours, for He shall change our vile body, that it may be fashioned like unto his glorious body (Php 3:21), and the believer’s hope is not a disembodied survival but a resurrection of this flesh. Toward the word: Psa 19:10 sets the honeycomb as the standard the Scriptures exceed, and the test is experimental. Pro 27:7 explains why so many find the Bible dull — the full soul loatheth an honeycomb. It is not that the comb has lost its sweetness; it is that the soul is stuffed with other food. Ezekiel ate the roll and it was in his mouth as honey for sweetness (Eze 3:3), and John did the same and found it bitter in the belly (Rev 10:10), for the word that delights also digests hard. And take the warning of Pro 5:3: the strange woman’s lips drop as an honeycomb too. Sweetness is not the test of truth; Scripture is.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Honey in the wax, unstrained; the measure of the word’s sweetness and a proof of the risen Lord’s true body.

expand to see more

Honeycomb — honey + comb; the waxen cells with the honey still in them.

Hebrew nopheth, the dropping comb (Psa 19:10; Pro 5:3; Pro 24:13).

Greek melission kerion, a comb of honey (Luk 24:42).

The comb exceeds strained honey as the word exceeds much fine gold.

Luk 24:42-43 is evidence, not decoration: a spirit hath not flesh and bones.

Usage

"Sweeter than honey and the honeycomb — the word’s worth measured against the sweetest thing known."

"The full soul loatheth an honeycomb: a dull Bible usually means a stuffed heart."

"He took it, and did eat before them — the honeycomb proves a real body raised."
